The Vendors Feature: How It Works

Finding a vendor, recommending one, getting your own service listed — and, for those who run similar efforts, an invitation.

The vendor directory is a resident-built, resident-powered guide to local services — more than 1,600 listings across 37 categories, shaped by the recommendations neighbors share. It is also a new service, and we are still working out the kinks — feedback of every kind is welcome. This page explains how to use it, how to help build it (including listing a service you run yourself), and what keeps it trustworthy. The last section is for residents who run other vendor-recommendation efforts in Sun City, with an invitation to collaborate.

Using the directory

Start at schh.info/vendors: every service category from plumbing to pet care to patios, with listings grouped, counted, and deep-linkable (e.g. /vendors/#plumbing). Each listing shows contact details, a short description, specialty tags, and how many residents have recommended or reported using the vendor.

  • Search wider when our list is thin. Inside any category you can run a Google-powered web search of nearby providers; those results are clearly labeled as not resident-recommended.
  • Or just ask. Signed-in residents can ask the Community Guide chat (“can anyone recommend a plumber?”, “who repairs bikes?”) and get resident recommendations alongside nearby options, with the same labeling.
  • Medical extras. Medical and dental listings carry additional research-sourced details, each shown with the date it was checked: whether the practice was accepting new patients — to the best of our knowledge when the listing was researched; practices change this often, so confirm when you call — along with Medicare acceptance, the hospitals CMS records associate with the practice’s clinicians, and the practitioners the federal NPI registry places there (the registry lags job changes, so treat it as what the registry says, not a current staff page). If what you find differs from a listing, please say so through the contact form — that is exactly the kind of correction that keeps the directory useful.

Help build it — it’s a community effort

Most of the directory’s listings were seeded by a category-by-category research pass — but research can only establish that a business exists and how to reach it. What makes a listing genuinely useful is a neighbor’s experience with it: the recommendations, corrections, and group-chat comments residents contribute. That layer is growing every week, and every contribution helps the next resident who searches. Three ways to pitch in, each taking a minute or two:

  • Recommend a vendor you’ve used. The recommendation form asks what the vendor did for you and how it went. Your name is never published — listings show only counts — but your recommendation makes the listing stronger for everyone.
  • Add a vendor that’s missing. Same form: if the vendor you want to recommend isn’t listed yet, your submission creates the listing (reviewed before it publishes).
  • Tell us what’s confusing or missing. This is a new service and rough edges remain. If a feature is unclear, hard to find, or hard to use — or there is something you wish the directory or the Guide could do in a future version — say so through the contact form. Resident feedback is how this gets better, and it genuinely shapes what gets built next.
  • Flag an error. Wrong phone number, closed business, wrong category, out-of-date description — send it through the contact form and it gets fixed. Had a genuinely bad experience? Report it privately — reports go only to the administrators, nothing negative is ever published, and repeated concerns about a vendor can lead to quiet removal.

Behind the scenes

Everything above rides one simple pipeline: recommend → review → publish.

  • Review. Every submission is reviewed by an administrator before it appears: names and categories are normalized, and anything inappropriate is filtered. Nothing publishes automatically.
  • One listing per vendor. When several residents recommend the same vendor, the submissions merge into a single listing: recommendation counts add up (“Recommended by 3 residents”), contact details fill in from whichever submission had them, and comments combine. Repeat recommendations make a listing stronger, not noisier.
  • Group-chat recommendations. With a group’s blessing, endorsements residents post in a participating community group chat (today, a Sun City services group on TeamReach) are gathered periodically and added to the matching listings — shown separately as recommendations “in a community group chat,” with a count and a few short quotes. Everything is anonymized before it is stored: names, phone numbers, and email addresses are removed from quotes, no poster’s identity is kept, and each resident counts once per vendor no matter how many times they mention it. A chat mention never changes the authenticated “residents report using” count — the two are labeled and counted separately. Want a comment of yours left out? Use the contact form and it will be removed.
  • “What residents mention.” When a listing has two or more resident comments — form notes, group-chat quotes, or both — an AI-written summary of the recurring themes appears. It is labeled AI-generated, restricted to what residents actually said, and reviewed by an administrator before publication.
  • Researched listings. Most listings were seeded by research rather than by a recommendation: each carries a one-line description, specialty tags, and — for medical practices — the dated details described under “Using the directory” above. The Online verification line (below) shows how much of a researched listing we could corroborate.

Resident-run services

Some of the most-recommended “vendors” in Sun City are neighbors: the resident who repairs bikes, does alterations, watches homes, or fixes a screen door. The directory lists them alongside commercial businesses, with a Resident-owned badge once ownership is verified — and with an extra layer of privacy: resident-run listings are shown only to signed-in residents, so a neighbor’s service is visible to the community, never to the open internet. If you offer a service yourself, submit it through the recommendation form — check the resident-owned box — or simply get in touch.

One rule we hold to: when a neighbor’s service is recommended in a group chat, the person is never listed automatically — or on anyone’s say-so but their own. Naming a resident in a public directory is different from naming a business, so those mentions go to a private follow-up list, and a listing is created only when the resident asks for it themselves (through the form above, or the contact page). We may reach out to let someone know their service has been recommended, but the request to be listed always comes from the resident.

Opting out

Everything here is opt-out on request, no questions asked. Through the contact form you can ask to:

  • Remove a comment of yours that was gathered from a participating group chat — the quote comes off the listing and out of the knowledge base.
  • Stop your chat posts being used at all going forward — your (anonymized) endorsements will no longer be added to listings.
  • Remove a mention of you as a service provider from the private follow-up list.
  • Take down your own listing, if you are a listed resident provider or business owner.

Comments are anonymized before anything is stored, so include a few words of the comment (or the vendor it was about) in your request and we’ll find it.

What “Online verification” means

Some listings carry a line reading Online verification with a small three-segment meter and one word — Extensive, Partial, or Limited. It answers one question only: how much of the listing could we corroborate from public online sources when it was researched? It is not a star rating, a quality score, or an endorsement of the vendor.

  • Extensive. Service in the Sun City area is reasonably confirmed, the business appears legitimate and active, a meaningful public record was found — reviews with real history, credentials — and licensing was checked where it applies.
  • Partial. The business appears legitimate and relevant, but a gap remains — for example, limited reviews, no explicit Sun City coverage confirmed, or licensing we could not verify.
  • Limited. We found the business but could not verify much about it. Check it out yourself — coverage, licensing, current operation — before hiring.

The line appears only on listings no resident has yet reported using. Once residents report using a vendor, that count is shown instead — a neighbor's actual experience says more than our homework does. The level is set by an administrator from source evidence and never moves automatically because a vendor gets recommended or becomes resident-owned. As with any listing here, use your own judgment when hiring — the meter describes how much we could verify, not a guarantee of the outcome.

How listings are ordered

Within a category, listings appear in this order:

  1. Resident-owned services come first.
  2. Then vendors at least one resident has personally recommended.
  3. Then by online verification — Extensive, then Partial, then Limited.
  4. Then by how many residents have recommended the vendor.
  5. Finally, alphabetically by name, as a tie-breaker.

Group-chat recommendation counts are shown on listings but do not currently affect this ordering — only authenticated recommendations move a listing up.

This is presentation order, not a ranking of who is “best.” A listing placed first because more residents happen to have recommended it is not necessarily the better fit for your particular job — read the listing, not just its position.

As of early September 2026 the directory holds more than 1,600 listings across 37 service categories, growing through the recommendation form and the participating group chat.

Research Briefs, briefly

A listing tells you a business exists and how to reach it. A Research Brief tells you what the public record actually says about it — and, just as important, what it doesn’t. A brief confirms the business’s identity against state business and licensing records, reports license status and public board actions with the date they were looked up (for medical practices, per clinician, with board certification where a board publishes it), attributes services and terms to their source, distills what independent reviews do and don’t show, and ends with the questions worth asking before you hire. Three finished briefs are live — Harbor Point Dentistry, Novant Health New Riverside Primary Care, and Bluffton Electric — and they show what to expect.

The rules are strict: every material statement traces to a source that was actually retrieved; an unknown is labeled “not verified,” never filled in; a lookup that shows no board orders is reported as exactly that, never as a clean record; there is no ranking, score, or endorsement; and medical and dental briefs stop at the consultation door — access, identity, licensure, and coverage, never clinical judgment.

The model is commissioned, then communal: a resident asks for a brief on a listing that doesn’t have one, and once the research passes its checks the brief joins the shared directory, readable by every verified resident. Paying for a brief buys priority and a contribution to the community — never a favorable conclusion. If the business can’t be identified with confidence or the evidence is too thin, no brief is published and the resident isn’t charged. Briefs are produced by AI-assisted research checked against official records and reviewed before publication. Commissioning isn’t open quite yet — the Research Briefs page explains what’s coming, and feedback on the finished examples helps shape it.

Other efforts, and an invitation

Vendor recommendations are among the most requested and most valuable information residents share — and among the worst-preserved. In most places they live in scrolling feeds and group chats: a great recommendation helps the people who happen to see it that week, then sinks, and six months later the same question is answered from memory or not at all. The most organized efforts go further — a dedicated volunteer collects submissions and assembles them into a shared list. That work proves how much residents value a real directory, and it deserves credit; it also shows the limits of hand assembly, which ages between updates and rests on one person’s continuing labor.

Sun City already has residents doing this work — notably the vendor-recommendation Facebook group and the TeamReach group. Those communities have something this system doesn't: active conversation, trust built over years, and a large accumulated body of recommendations. This system has what the feeds lack: permanence, structure, search, and a home that any resident can reach without joining anything.

As of September 2026 that collaboration is no longer hypothetical: with one TeamReach services group, endorsements shared in the group now flow into the directory’s listings (see “Group-chat recommendations” above), and the group’s accumulated history — hundreds of endorsements across well over a hundred vendors — was reviewed and folded in.

Those are complementary strengths, not competing ones. The groups are where recommendations happen; this can be where they last. Some concrete forms collaboration could take, in increasing order of ambition:

  • Cross-linking. The groups point members at the vendors page as the durable reference; the guide points residents who want discussion toward the groups.
  • Importing the archive — where that's possible. Where an administrator already maintains an assembled list of their group's recommendations, that list could — with their blessing — be reviewed and folded into the structured directory, preserving years of community knowledge in one step. Where platform rules make exporting past posts impractical, the path is prospective instead: the group shares a link to the recommendation form and encourages members to submit there in addition to posting in the group — the conversation stays where it lives, and the recommendation also lands somewhere permanent.
  • Shared stewardship. Group administrators — some of whom already collect and assemble recommendations by hand — are exactly the right people to help review submissions, watch categories they know well, or shape policy. This system automates the assembly, publishing, merging, and counting; the human judgment stays, shared among more hands.
  • Consolidation, if and when it earns it. If this system proves itself the better home, groups could retire their parallel record-keeping in its favor — on their timeline, by their choice.

Design choices, for those who have wrestled with the same trade-offs

  • Curated, not open-posting. Open forums self-moderate through volume; a directory can't. Review-before- publish keeps quality high, keeps spam and self-promotion out, and means every listing is accountable to a named (but unpublished) recommender.
  • Positive-or-absent — no published negatives. Publishing complaints about named local businesses invites disputes and legal exposure that a resident-run effort should not carry, and one-sided accounts presented as fact don't serve residents either. Instead, concerns are collected privately, patterns are watched, and the consequence is quiet removal. On a curated list, absence is the signal.
  • Verified residents, private identities. Recommending and reporting require resident sign-in — so every input is accountable — but recommender and reporter names are never published or shared. Listings show only counts.
  • Structured records, not threads. A recommendation captured as data (category, contacts, count) can be browsed, searched, merged, counted, and cited by the chat assistant. A recommendation captured as a chat message can only be scrolled past.
  • The web search knows its place. The wider Google search is bounded to our service categories (which keeps its costs controlled and predictable) and its results are always labeled as not resident-recommended. It supplements the community's knowledge; it never impersonates it.
  • No platform lock-in. The entire vendor database can be exported by an administrator to an ordinary spreadsheet at any time. If this effort ever ends or changes hands, the community's accumulated recommendations are a file, not a hostage.

If you help run one of these efforts and any of this interests you — or you think parts of it are wrong — please reach out through the contact form. Skeptical feedback is as welcome as enthusiasm; you know failure modes of this work that I haven't hit yet.

The guide is an independent, resident-created project — not an official Community Association service. Vendor listings are a convenience, not an endorsement; residents should use their own judgment when hiring. See the about page for the full picture.
